name: Córdoba
tagline: The caliphs' city of three faiths
intro: A thousand years ago Córdoba was one of the largest and most learned cities in Europe — capital of al-Andalus, where Muslims, Jews and Christians shaped one city together. Its streets still mix all three.

lessons.title: A forest of striped arches
lessons.hook: Step inside the Mosque–Cathedral and let your eyes adjust: rows upon rows of columns, holding up double arches that seem to go on for ever.
lessons.challenge: What two colours stripe the arches?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says red (brick/terracotta) and white (stone/cream), in either order or any language.
hints: Look up at the stripes on the arches, not the columns.
One colour is brick, the other is stone.
lessons.story: Building began in 785 under Abd al-Rahman I, the Umayyad prince who escaped to Spain and founded a new state. Stacking two arches was an innovation: it let the roof rise high on fairly short columns, many reused from Roman and Visigothic buildings. The stripes alternate red brick and white stone. After the Christian conquest of 1236 it became a cathedral, and in the 16th century a Renaissance church was built right in the middle of the forest of columns.

lessons.title: Two thousand years over the river
lessons.hook: Walk out onto the long stone bridge across the Guadalquivir, with the Mosque–Cathedral behind you.
lessons.challenge: Count them: how many arches carry the bridge?
hints: Lean over the side, or count from the riverbank.
lessons.story: The Romans built a stone bridge here in the early 1st century BC, and for centuries it was the city's only way across the river. It was rebuilt many times, especially in the Islamic period, and today stands on 16 arches — one fewer than at first. At the far end is the Calahorra Tower, a medieval gatehouse that now holds a museum about Córdoba's three cultures.

sources.label: The Roman Bridge of Cordoba — Ancient Origins

lessons.title: The philosopher in the Jewish Quarter
lessons.hook: In the lanes of the Judería there's a tiny square with a seated bronze figure in a turban, a book on his lap.
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player names Maimonides (Moses ben Maimon, Rambam).
hints: The name is carved on the statue's base.
He was a Jewish philosopher and doctor, born in this city.
lessons.story: Maimonides was born in Córdoba in 1138 and became one of the greatest Jewish thinkers — a philosopher and physician who wrote in Arabic and Hebrew. He left as a young man when the Almohads persecuted non-Muslims, and died in Egypt; he is buried in Tiberias, which is why this little square is called Plaza de Tiberíades. A few steps away stands the synagogue of 1315, one of only three medieval synagogues left in Spain.

lessons.title: Where Columbus pitched his plan
lessons.hook: Walk through the Alcázar's long gardens of pools, orange trees and clipped hedges. Look for a statue group of three people.
lessons.challenge: The statue shows Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand listening to an explorer. Who is he?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player names Christopher Columbus (Cristóbal Colón).
hints: He's holding a map or plans in front of the monarchs.
Six years after this meeting he sailed west, in 1492.
lessons.story: Ferdinand and Isabella used this fortress-palace as a base during their war against Granada. In 1486 a Genoese sailor, Christopher Columbus, had his first audience with them here and asked for ships to reach Asia by sailing west. They made him wait: the answer came in 1492. The Alcázar later housed the Inquisition and, after that, a prison.

lessons.title: The street of flowers
lessons.hook: Find the narrow, whitewashed Calleja de las Flores near the Mosque–Cathedral. Walk to the little square at its end, then turn around.
lessons.challenge: What covers the white walls of the alley?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says flowers, flowerpots or plants (geraniums, carnations).
hints: Look up at the walls, not the ground.
They're bright red and hang all over the walls.
lessons.story: Córdoba's houses are built around cool inner patios — a tradition with Roman and Islamic roots — and families fill them with pots of geraniums and carnations. Every May the city holds its Patios Festival, when people open their courtyards to visitors; it is recognised by UNESCO. And from the end of this alley, the bell tower of the Mosque–Cathedral is framed perfectly between the white walls.

sources.label: Calleja de las Flores — Córdoba tourism

lessons.title: A square for everything
lessons.hook: Step into the Plaza de la Corredera, a huge rectangle closed on all four sides by arcades and rows of balconies.
lessons.challenge: Long before the cafés, the square was used as an arena. For what kind of spectacle?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says bullfights (accept any language).
hints: The balconies were the best seats in the house.
Think of Spain's most famous — and most argued-about — spectacle.
lessons.story: La Corredera took its arcaded shape in the 17th century and became the city's stage: markets, festivals, bullfights watched from the balconies, and even public punishments ordered by the Inquisition. Squares like this are typical of central Spain and rare in Andalusia. Today the arcades shelter cafés, and the square still hosts Córdoba's celebrations.

sources.label: Plaza de la Corredera — Lonely Planet
